archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: A 38-year-old journeyman who wins on structure: under-center play-action, short and intermediate throws over the middle, and getting the ball out before the rush arrives, without the arm to threaten deep or the creativity to rescue a broken play.

report.headline: Ran Ben Johnson's script well in one start; can't carry obvious passing downs.
report.take:
Keenum is the Bears' QB3 as of October 20, behind a healthy Caleb Williams, so his 2026 is a two-game snapshot of what Chicago gets when the depth chart runs out. The snapshot splits cleanly in two. In the Week 3 start against Philadelphia he was a tidy distributor: 24 of 34, 247 yards, two touchdowns, 0.213 EPA per dropback, a 2.41-second release and pressure on only 8.6% of dropbacks. In the Week 5 relief appearance at Green Bay, inside a 7-31 loss, he went 11 of 19 for 108 with an interception, a lost fumble and a 31.6% bad-throw rate.

What separates those games is the kind of football he was asked to play, more than his own form. On 14 under-center plays he completed 92.9% with 0.818 EPA per play and a 25.4 CPOE. Those are play-action and boot concepts where the scheme makes the read for him. On 41 shotgun plays he fell to -0.394 EPA and a -8.9 CPOE. The game-state split tells the same story: 0.35 EPA per play within one score, -0.568 when trailing by nine or more. He functions when Johnson can stay on schedule and run the offense through the middle of the field. He sinks when the defense knows he has to throw.

The season line hides how narrow his useful range is. His 3.6% sack rate ranks 4th of 45 and his pressure rate 3rd of 37, which looks like pocket mastery. It is mostly the quick, short game. When pressure did get home, 28.6% of it became sacks (23rd of 37). Beyond 20 air yards he went 1 of 4 for -0.816 EPA per attempt, and his 17% bad-throw rate ranks 33rd of 37. The 2017 Vikings season, with 0.174 EPA per play and a 3.6 CPOE, was the outlier of his career. Most years sit near or below zero, and his last stint before this, in 2023, came in at -0.265.

The outlook is simple. Keenum only matters again if Williams goes down, and even then the Bears might turn to Tyson Bagent, who started Week 5. If he does play, expect the Philly version in friendly scripts and the Green Bay version when Chicago falls behind.

strengths.title: Thrives under center, on schedule
strengths.body: His best football came on under-center dropbacks and in one-score games, where play-action and defined reads let him throw on rhythm. It is a 14-play sample, so the rates are inflated, but the direction fits his whole career: he is a scheme-dependent passer who executes a good plan cleanly. In Ben Johnson's offense that structure will be there as long as the score stays close.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws over the middle
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards produced 0.734 EPA per attempt, and passes to the middle of the field added 0.35 EPA a play with both of his touchdowns. Those are seams and digs behind linebackers, the throws a veteran with anticipation can still make. On 11 intermediate attempts this is a hint, not a fact, but it is the one area where his arm still creates value.

strengths.title: Gets it out, keeps sacks down
strengths.body: A 2.41-second release in his start kept him clean, and his overall sack rate sits well under the league's 6.8%. That comes from design and quick decisions, not from escapability. It holds up as long as the offense stays in rhythm.

concerns.title: Collapses in obvious passing situations
concerns.body: Out of the shotgun and while trailing big, his efficiency fell off a cliff, with two sacks, his interception and a negative CPOE. Part of that is the context of a 31-7 hole at Green Bay. Still, he has no way to manufacture explosive plays once defenses can tee off. This is who he has been for years, not a blip.

concerns.title: No vertical game, loose accuracy
concerns.body: He rarely throws deep and hit one of four when he did, and his bad-throw rate ranks near the bottom of qualifiers. Rome Odunze, the outside receiver who should stretch the field, cost -7.3 EPA on 11 targets with Keenum. That tells you the outside and deep shots are where this offense dies with him under center. At 38.7, that ceiling won't rise.

concerns.title: Career baseline is below average
concerns.body: Strip out 2017 and his career EPA per play mostly sits around or below zero. His last action before this year, in 2023, was poor. The Philadelphia start came against a defense now ranked 25th, so the good half of his sample was earned against soft resistance.

trend.note: An efficient full start against a weak Philly defense, then a rough partial game in a blowout at Green Bay. With Williams back as the starter in Week 6 and Keenum listed third, there is no live trend to follow.

nextGame.headline: QB3 behind a healthy Williams: not expected to play against New England
nextGame.body:
Keenum is third on the depth chart as of October 20, so his Thursday role against the Patriots is emergency-only. If he were forced in, the matchup would suit what he does: New England is middling against the pass (13th in pass EPA allowed, 24th on deep throws) and has given up 0.44 EPA per target to opposing WR1s. Its tight end coverage, though, ranks 3rd, which closes off one of the middle-of-the-field targets he leans on. With Chicago a 3-point favorite and the total at 50.5, the expected script is close. That is the state where he has been effective, not the catch-up mode that sank him.

Availability on both sides tilts toward Chicago's passing game, whoever throws. Starting corner Carlton Davis III (95% of snaps) is out for New England, along with two depth corners, which thins the outside coverage where Keenum struggled most. On Chicago's side, guard Jonah Jackson (94% of snaps) is questionable with a hip. Losing him would hurt the interior pocket that Keenum's quick middle game depends on. Running back Kyle Monangai is out, which leans more on Roschon Johnson. None of it changes Keenum's outlook unless Williams is hurt.

keyMatchups.title: Patriots' depleted cornerback room
keyMatchups.body: With Davis out and two reserve corners sidelined, New England's outside coverage is thin on a short week. That helps any Bears passer, but especially one whose outside throws to the right have cost -6.1 EPA.

keyMatchups.title: Jonah Jackson's hip and interior protection
keyMatchups.body: Keenum's game rests on a clean interior pocket for quick middle throws. With Jackson questionable, a backup guard would invite the inside pressure he converts to sacks at a below-average rate.

keyMatchups.title: Tight-end lane closed
keyMatchups.body: New England has held top tight ends well under their averages and to negative EPA per target. That squeezes Colston Loveland, one of the middle-of-the-field options this kind of passer relies on.

nextGame.watch: Caleb Williams's health. Keenum only takes snaps if Williams goes down, and even then Bagent may be next in line.

restOfSeason.body:
The base case is no meaningful action: he is the third quarterback on a team with a healthy starter. If injuries push him back into a start, expect roughly his Philly profile when Chicago can stay balanced and under center: a short-to-intermediate distributor with a low sack rate, a completion rate near league average and few big plays. Expect the Green Bay profile when the Bears trail.

The under-center and one-score efficiency won't hold at those levels. Those are 14- and 29-play samples, and his career says he settles into a slightly below-average passer. The low sack rate is the most sustainable piece because it comes from the quick game. The deep-ball weakness and the scattered bad throws are permanent at this stage.

projections.stat: Pass EPA per dropback (if he starts)

swingFactors: Whether Bagent or Keenum is the first call-up
Game script: close games vs. catch-up mode

confidence.note: Two games, one a partial blowout appearance; QB3 role means little future playing time.
